blocks.text: The recording of electrical potentials, generated by the currents of cardiac impulses, is known as electrocardiogram (ECG). When cardiac impulse passes over the surface of heart, a minute electrical current is generated. This current spreads into the tissues surrounding heart. This minute electrical current also travels to the surface of body. In ECG, the electrical potentials generated by this current are measured and recorded. For this purpose, electrodes are placed on skin on the opposite sides of heart. The electrodes are attached to a machine called electrocardiograph that records electrical potentials generated by this current. ECG helps to diagnose the abnormalities in conduction system of heart. ECG shows the following waves of electrical impulses produced at specific events of cardiac cycle. (Figure 11.5).

blocks.alt: Top: one ECG trace with a small P wave, a flat PR segment, the tall QRS complex, a flat ST segment and a rounded T wave; a bracket marks the QT interval. Below: six small hearts, each beside the trace with the matching part coloured, show depolarisation (orange) spreading from the SA node through the atria and AV node to the ventricles, then repolarisation (red) of the ventricles during the T wave.
blocks.caption: Figure 11.5: ECG reading of a single heartbeat (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 11.5).
blocks.long_description: Labels: P, PR, QRS, ST, T, QT interval, SA node, AV node, Depolarisation, Repolarisation.

blocks.text: P wave: It shows beginning of atrial depolarization, initiated by SA node. It causes atrial contraction. Irregular or absent P waves may indicate arrhythmia (lack of rhythmicity).
PR segment: It shows the completion of atrial depolarization. It is usually 0.12 to 0.20 seconds. A prolonged PR indicates a first-degree heart block.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book gives 0.12 to 0.20 seconds for the PR segment. That is the normal PR interval (from the start of the P wave to the start of the QRS complex). The PR segment (from the end of the P wave to the start of QRS) is shorter, about 0.05 to 0.12 seconds. A first-degree heart block is a prolonged PR interval (more than 0.20 seconds).

QRS: It shows the beginning of depolarization of ventricles. Atrial re-polarization also occurs during this phase. Abnormalities in the QRS complex may indicate bundle branch block, ventricular tachycardia (faster rate of contraction), or other ventricular abnormalities.

Some abnormal babies may have blueness (cyanosis) of skin. They are called blue babies. It is due to the mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood between two atria. Mixed blood is supplied to the body of new born babies resulting in blueness of skin. Cyanosis results due to the failure of interatrial foramen to close, during development. Interatrial foramen is a temporary opening in the embryonic heart between right and left atria. Normally, it is closed during development. Cyanosis may also happen due to failure of ductus arteriosus to fully constrict, during development. Ductus arteriosus is a temporary channel between the embryonic pulmonary artery and aorta. Normally, it constricts during development.

ST segment: It shows the completion of depolarization of ventricles. It can be depressed in ischemia (decreased flow of blood and oxygen to heart muscles) and elevated in myocardial infarction. This segment ordinarily lasts about 0.08 second.

T wave: It represents the beginning of repolarization of ventricles. T wave abnormalities may indicate electrolyte disturbance. The hyper-acute T wave shows the earliest findings of acute myocardial infarction.
QT interval: The QT interval is from the beginning of the QRS complex to the end of the T wave. A normal QT interval is usually about 0.40 seconds.
